prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A professor invites me to his “Black Lit” class; they’re reading Larson’s Passing. One of the black students says, “Sometimes light-skinned blacks think they can fool other blacks, but I can always tell,” looking right through me. After I tell them I am black, I ask the class, “Was I passing when I was just sitting here, before I told you?” A white woman shakes her head desperately, as if I had deliberately deceived her. She keeps examining my face, then turning away as if she hopes I’ll disappear. Why presume “passing” is based on what I leave out and not what she fills in? In one scene in the book, in a restaurant, she’s “passing,” though no one checked her at the door— “Hey, you black?” My father, who looked white, told me this story: every year when he’d go to get his driver’s license, the man at the window filling out the form would ask, “White or black?” pencil poised, without looking up. My father wouldn’t pass, but he might use silence to trap a devil. When he didn’t speak, the man would look up at my father’s face. “What did he write?” my father quizzed me.

A professor asks me to visit his “Black Lit” course, where the students are studying Larsen’s *Passing*. During the discussion, one Black student remarks, “Sometimes light-skinned blacks think they can fool other blacks, but I can always tell,” and she looks straight through me as she says it.  

Once I tell the class that I am Black, I ask them, “Before I said anything, when I was only sitting here, was I passing?” A white woman shakes her head with an almost frantic denial, as though I had intentionally misled her. She keeps studying my face and then looking away, as if wishing I would vanish. But why assume that “passing” depends on what I fail to disclose rather than on what she chooses to imagine?  

In one scene from the novel, set in a restaurant, a character is understood to be “passing,” even though no one stopped her at the entrance to ask, “Hey, are you Black?”  

My father, who appeared white, once told me a story. Each year, when he went to renew his driver’s license, the clerk behind the window would fill out the form and ask, without raising his eyes, “White or black?” His pencil would be waiting for the answer. My father would not pass, but he might let silence corner a devil. When he stayed quiet, the clerk would finally look up and see my father’s face.  

“What did he put down?” my father would ask me, testing me.
outputs.L3:
A professor once invited the narrator to speak to a Black literature class in which the students were reading Nella Larsen’s *Passing*. The novel, with its focus on race, appearance, secrecy, and social perception, provided the occasion for a conversation about what it means to “pass” and how racial identity is recognized—or misrecognized—by others.

During the discussion, a Black student confidently claimed that she could always identify light-skinned Black people. The narrator challenged this assumption by quietly revealing that she herself was Black. This moment unsettled the student’s certainty and exposed the limits of visual judgment. If the student had not recognized the narrator as Black until being told, then her confidence in being able to “see” racial identity was called into question.

The episode leads the narrator to reflect on the nature of passing itself. Is passing defined by what a person deliberately hides, or is it created by what other people assume? The narrator suggests that passing may not always depend on deception by the person being observed. Instead, it may arise from the expectations, projections, and racial categories that others impose. If people decide that someone is white because of appearance, speech, class position, or behavior, then the act of “passing” may be as much about their assumptions as about the individual’s concealment.

This dynamic becomes especially clear in the reaction of a white woman in the class. After learning that the narrator is Black, the woman appears uncomfortable and begins to scrutinize her more closely, as though searching for evidence she had previously missed. Her reaction suggests that she feels somehow deceived, even though the narrator had not necessarily lied or claimed to be white. The discomfort comes from the collapse of the woman’s assumptions: she had read the narrator in one way, and now she must confront the fact that her reading was wrong.

The narrator connects this experience to her father, who also looked white. On official forms or in situations where racial identity had to be declared, he often used silence strategically. Rather than immediately identifying himself, he allowed others to reveal their assumptions about him. His silence became a way of exposing how racial classification often depends less on truth than on perception. By withholding an answer, he forced others to confront the categories they imposed and the confidence with which they assigned race based on appearance.

Together, these moments show that passing is not simply a matter of pretending to be something one is not. It is also a social process shaped by the expectations and desires of observers. The narrator’s experience in the classroom, the white woman’s reaction, and her father’s quiet challenges to official racial identification all reveal how unstable and constructed racial perception can be.
outputs.L4:
Racial “passing” is often described as an individual act of disguise: a person with one racial identity is imagined to be intentionally hiding it in order to be accepted as another. But this way of thinking places too much emphasis on the person who is supposedly passing and not enough on the people and systems doing the seeing. Passing is not only about concealment. It is also about perception, assumption, and classification. A person “passes” because others decide what they are looking at, often quickly and confidently, based on appearance, behavior, name, language, or context. In that sense, passing reveals that race is not simply something a person is, but something that is socially read, assigned, and enforced.

A classroom encounter can make this especially clear. When someone’s racial identity is assumed incorrectly by classmates or a teacher, the mistake often says more about the observers than about the person being observed. The person has not necessarily hidden anything. They may simply have entered a space where others relied on their own expectations about what race is supposed to look like. A student might be treated as white, Black, Latinx, Asian, Indigenous, or “ambiguous” depending on skin tone, hair texture, accent, last name, clothing, or even the racial makeup of the room. These assumptions can change from one setting to another. The same person may be read differently in different communities, which shows how unstable racial perception can be.

This instability is central to Nella Larsen’s novel *Passing*. In the novel, Clare Kendry and Irene Redfield are both light-skinned Black women, but they navigate racial identity in different ways. Clare lives much of her adult life passing as white, even marrying a racist white man who does not know she is Black. Irene, by contrast, identifies and lives as a Black woman, though she too can move through certain white spaces because of her appearance. Larsen does not present passing as a simple matter of truth versus deception. Instead, the novel shows how racial identity depends on social recognition. Clare is accepted as white because the white people around her believe she is white. Their belief becomes a kind of temporary reality, even though it is built on ignorance and racial fantasy.

The danger in *Passing* comes from the fact that racial categories are socially enforced. Clare’s life depends on other people continuing to read her in a particular way. Her husband’s racism makes this especially threatening: if he were to classify her differently, her social position, marriage, and safety would collapse. This reveals the violence behind racial perception. Being “seen” as one race or another is not neutral. It can determine where a person is allowed to live, whom they can marry, what work they can do, and whether they are treated with dignity or suspicion. Larsen’s novel demonstrates that passing is not merely a private choice but a response to a society that attaches material consequences to racial categories.

A family anecdote about bureaucratic racial classification points to the same problem from another angle. In official documents, race is often treated as if it were obvious, stable, and easily recorded. A form may require a box to be checked, a clerk may assign a category, or a government record may label a person according to the assumptions of the time. Yet these classifications can be arbitrary. One family member might be recorded as one race on a birth certificate, another as a different race on a census form, and another as something else entirely depending on who filled out the paperwork. The person’s identity may not have changed at all, but the official record changes because the system demands a category and someone has the power to impose one.

This kind of bureaucratic labeling shows that race is not only perceived socially but also administered institutionally. Once written into records, racial classification can follow families across generations. It can affect citizenship, schooling, housing, employment, inheritance, and legal rights. The fact that a clerk or official could assign a racial identity demonstrates that race has often functioned less as a biological fact than as a tool of social organization and control. Bureaucracy gives racial assumptions the appearance of truth. A category written on a document can seem authoritative, even if it began as someone’s guess.

Together, the classroom encounter, Larsen’s *Passing*, and the family anecdote show that passing is not simply about a person pretending to be something they are not. It is about the way other people interpret bodies and the way institutions turn those interpretations into social facts. A person may be “passed” by others without trying to pass at all. They may be misread, simplified, or forced into a category that does not reflect their own understanding of themselves. Race, then, is revealed as something produced through interaction: it is seen, assumed, recorded, and enforced.

This does not mean race is unreal. On the contrary, the consequences of racial classification are very real. What these examples show is that race is socially constructed, not imaginary. Its power comes from the fact that people and institutions act as though racial categories are natural and self-evident. Passing exposes the fragility of that belief. If race can be misread, reassigned, or bureaucratically changed, then it cannot be the fixed biological truth it has often been claimed to be. Instead, it is a system of meaning imposed on bodies, maintained through perception, and backed by social and institutional power.
outputs.L5:
**Black Lit and Larson: A Reflection**

Black literature, often called **Black Lit**, is a powerful tradition that gives voice to the histories, struggles, creativity, and resilience of Black communities. It includes poetry, novels, essays, drama, and memoirs that explore identity, racism, culture, freedom, and self-expression. Through storytelling, Black writers have challenged stereotypes, preserved cultural memory, and created space for new ways of understanding the world.

When thinking about Black Lit, the name **Larson** can be connected to the importance of studying and discussing literature through different perspectives. Whether referring to a scholar, teacher, or reader, Larson represents the role of interpretation: asking questions, analyzing themes, and helping others see the deeper meaning within a text. Literature becomes more than words on a page; it becomes a conversation between the writer, the reader, and society.

Black Lit continues to be relevant because it speaks to both past and present realities. It reminds us that stories matter, representation matters, and voices that were once ignored must be heard. Through authors, critics, and readers like Larson, Black literature remains alive, meaningful, and lit with truth, beauty, and resistance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person literary nonfiction passage about being invited to a Black literature class discussing Nella Larsen’s *Passing*, exploring racial ambiguity, misrecognition, and the narrator’s father’s driver’s license story.
counterfactuals.output:
When I was invited to speak to a Black literature class about Nella Larsen’s *Passing*, I thought first of my father’s driver’s license.

Not the man himself, not yet—though he is never far from any room where race is being discussed with the lights on and the windows open—but the small laminated card he carried in his wallet, creased at the edges, its photograph flattened into state-issued certainty. There was a line on it, a box checked by someone behind a counter, someone who had looked up at my father’s face and decided what the state needed him to be.

White.

He had told me the story more than once, sometimes with amusement, sometimes with a kind of weary disbelief. He had gone to renew his license, stood where he was told to stand, answered what he was asked, and when the card arrived, there it was: the official misrecognition. Not an error of height or weight, not a misspelled name, but a racial designation that seemed to expose the absurdity of the whole enterprise while also reminding him of its power. A stranger had looked at him and seen wrong—or perhaps had seen exactly what America has trained itself to see when it wants simplicity more than truth.

I carried that story with me into the classroom.

The students had been reading Larsen’s 1929 novel, that slim, volatile book in which looking becomes a form of danger. *Passing* is a novel about women who are seen and unseen, who move through the world under the pressure of other people’s assumptions. Clare Kendry crosses the color line not as metaphor but as daily practice, marrying a white man who does not know—or does not allow himself to know—that she is Black. Irene Redfield, safer, more respectable, more invested in boundaries, is drawn toward Clare with fascination, disapproval, and fear. Around them, race appears not as essence but as performance, as arrangement, as a perilous agreement between the body and the gaze.

The students sat around the room with marked-up books and open laptops, their faces bright with that particular intensity young people bring to old texts when they discover the oldness is a disguise. They wanted to talk about passing, of course, but also about desire, class, motherhood, betrayal, Harlem, marriage, the strange heat between Clare and Irene. They wanted to know whether Clare was free or trapped, whether Irene hated Clare or wanted her, whether the ending was accident, murder, suicide, or something more terrible because it remained undecided.

I listened, and I thought again of the license.

My father was not passing. That distinction mattered to me. He had not set out to deceive anyone, had not slipped into whiteness as strategy or escape. He was simply standing in a government office, being himself, while someone else’s categories failed around him. And yet the card told a story he had not authored. It granted him, falsely, a proximity to whiteness that could not be separated from the history of what such proximity has meant: safety, mobility, presumption, the benefit of the doubt. Even as the error insulted him, it revealed something. Race, for all its brutality, is also bureaucratic. It is written down. It is checked off. It is placed in files. It is made to look obvious after the fact.

In Larsen’s novel, racial ambiguity is never merely visual. It is social, atmospheric. It gathers around speech, neighborhood, clothing, gesture, who knows your mother, who remembers your childhood, who is permitted to ask questions and who is expected to answer them. Clare can pass not because race is unreal, but because race in America has always depended on a violent mixture of fantasy and enforcement. She passes because whiteness is willing to believe in itself. She passes because people see what protects them.

That was what I told the class, or tried to.

I said that misrecognition is not always accidental. Sometimes it is a wish. Sometimes it is a convenience. Sometimes it is the first move in a larger theft. To be misrecognized can feel like erasure, but it can also reveal the instability of the recognizer, the fragility of the categories they depend on. My father’s license did not change who he was. But it changed, however briefly, the record of him. It produced a version of him legible to the state and false to his life.

The students nodded, some slowly, some with the expression of people measuring the distance between literature and their own families. That is the thing about a book like *Passing*: it does not stay in 1929. It walks into the present tense and begins opening drawers. It asks who has been mistaken for what, who has been allowed to become a stranger to themselves, who has survived by being unreadable.

I wanted to say that I come from people who have been read incorrectly and too well, both. People whose bodies have been made into evidence. People who know that the eye is not innocent. The eye carries law, appetite, fear, memory. It carries the census, the plantation, the school form, the police report, the marriage certificate, the driver’s license. It carries the old hunger to sort human beings into punishable and protected categories.

But I also wanted to leave room for opacity. For the right not to be fully known. Clare’s ambiguity unsettles because it refuses the comfort of stable interpretation. Irene wants to place her. Readers want to place her. The world wants to place her. Yet Clare remains dazzling and dangerous partly because she exceeds the terms available to describe her. My father, too, exceeded the box. Not by trying, not by performance, but by existing beyond the convenience of another person’s glance.

After class, I thought about how often we ask literature to clarify what life has made murky. But Larsen does something braver. She lets murk remain murk. She understands that racial categories can be both invented and deadly, both incoherent and enforced. She understands that a mistake on a document is not just a mistake when the document belongs to a country with a long memory for blood.

My father laughed when he told the story, but beneath the laughter was the knowledge that a stranger’s error had touched an old wound. The license was small enough to fit in his wallet. The history behind it was not.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective memoir-style scene in which a light-skinned Black narrator attends a class on *Passing* and questions whether “passing” depends on deception or on other people’s assumptions.
counterfactuals.output:
The first time we discussed *Passing* in class, the room felt too bright.

It was one of those seminar rooms with windows on one side and a long table in the center, the kind of room that made everyone’s face visible whether they wanted it or not. February light slanted across our notebooks. Someone had brought coffee in a paper cup that softened and bent at the rim. I remember the smell of it—burnt and familiar—because I needed something ordinary to hold on to.

We were halfway through Nella Larsen’s novel when our professor wrote the word on the board:

**PASSING**

She underlined it once, then turned back to us.

“What does it require?” she asked. “What makes passing possible?”

There was the usual seminar pause, not silence exactly, but the sound of people arranging themselves into readiness: pens clicking, pages turning, throats clearing. Across from me, a white girl in a wool sweater raised her hand and said, “Deception.”

The word landed cleanly, confidently.

I looked down at my copy of the book, at the cover curled from being carried in my bag. Deception. It was a word with a sharp little hook in it. It made the passer into a magician, a liar, someone slipping through a door by pretending to be invited. It made passing sound like an act performed alone.

Our professor nodded. “Say more.”

“Well,” the girl said, “Clare is hiding who she really is. She’s making people believe she’s white.”

A few students nodded. I could feel, rather than see, the classroom settle around that answer. It was a reasonable answer. It was the answer we had all been taught to expect.

Still, something in me resisted.

I was light-skinned enough that people had been wrong about me all my life, though rarely in ways that felt neutral. In grocery stores, cashiers spoke to my mother with one tone and to me with another, then glanced between us as if trying to solve a puzzle we had rudely brought into public. At school, children asked what I was before they asked my name. In college, strangers guessed me into categories with the ease of people tossing keys into a bowl: Latina, mixed, Mediterranean, “something.” Once, at a party, a boy told me I looked “racially ambiguous” with the satisfaction of someone offering a compliment. When I told him I was Black, he blinked.

“Really?” he said.

As if I had contradicted his eyes.

I did not pass for white, not exactly. Or maybe I had, sometimes, without knowing it. Maybe that was part of what unsettled me: passing was often discussed as if it required intention, a plan, a costume. But what do you call it when someone looks at you and builds the costume themselves?

I raised my hand before I had decided what to say.

My professor looked at me. “Yes?”

“I’m not sure it always starts with deception,” I said.

The room shifted. Not dramatically. Just enough.

I felt my face grow warm, which irritated me. I was used to being looked at, but not always used to choosing it.

“I mean,” I continued, “Clare does lie. Obviously. But I keep thinking about how much of passing depends on other people wanting the lie—or not even seeing it as a lie because they’ve already decided what race looks like.”

My professor leaned against the edge of the desk. “That’s interesting. Can you explain?”

I pressed my thumb into the margin of the book. “If someone assumes you’re white because your skin is light, or because your hair is a certain texture, or because you’re in a certain neighborhood, then is the first act really yours? Or is it theirs?”

No one answered right away.

I could hear a radiator knocking in the wall.

Then a Black student at the end of the table—darker-skinned than me, quiet most weeks—said, “But if you don’t correct them, isn’t that still a choice?”

I turned toward her. I knew she was right. I also knew the question had teeth.

“Yes,” I said. “Sometimes. But even correcting people can become a whole performance. You have to decide when to interrupt the story they’ve made up about you. And whether it’s worth what comes after.”

What came after: the double take, the apology too loud to be sincere, the sudden inventory of features. People searching your face for evidence. People asking about your parents, your grandparents, your “real” background, as though Blackness had to be notarized.

When I was twelve, a substitute teacher marked me absent while I sat in the second row. She called my name, paused, and looked around the room. I raised my hand.

“That’s you?” she said.

The class laughed, not cruelly at first, but laughter has a way of becoming cruel once it knows where to go.

“Yes,” I said.

She looked at the attendance sheet again, then at me. “Oh. I thought—” She stopped.

Everyone knew what she thought. Or thought they did.

That afternoon, I came home angry in a way I could not explain. My mother was in the kitchen cutting onions, the radio low behind her. I told her the story like it was funny, because that was how I had learned to carry certain things. She put down the knife and looked at me for a long moment.

“People will try to tell you what you are,” she said. “Don’t help them.”

At the time, I thought she meant I should be firm. Later, I wondered if she meant something more complicated: that I did not owe every stranger a family tree, a correction, a confession.

In the classroom, the conversation had quickened. Someone mentioned Irene’s jealousy, someone else the danger Clare lived with, the violence of being found out. The girl in the wool sweater said, “But Clare benefits from it. She gets access to whiteness.”

Access. Another clean word for a dirty arrangement.

I wrote it in my notebook and circled it.

There was no denying the benefit. That was the ache of it. Passing could be survival, ambition, betrayal, self-erasure, escape. It could be all of these at once. It could open doors that should never have been closed. It could also require you to stand on the other side and pretend not to hear the knocking.

But I kept thinking about the people guarding those doors.

About how confidently they decided who belonged.

About how whiteness, in the novel and outside it, often behaved less like an identity than a property line: fenced, patrolled, inherited, defended. And yet the fence had gaps. Not because it was generous, but because it was imaginary in the first place.

My professor asked us to look at a passage where Clare moves through a white social world undetected. Around me, pages whispered open. I found the paragraph, but my mind slipped elsewhere—to department stores where no one followed me until I arrived with darker-skinned cousins; to relatives who joked that I had “gotten the light genes,” as if inheritance were a lottery ticket; to the summer I spent avoiding the sun because I was tired of people announcing changes in my complexion like weather reports.

I thought of my grandmother, who was lighter than all of us and still never mistaken for anything but what she was. Maybe it was how she carried herself, or where she lived, or the generation she came from, or the fact that the world had fewer categories available to soften its gaze. In old photographs, she looked almost translucent, her face framed by cat-eye glasses, her expression direct and unsmiling. Nobody in the family ever said she passed. They said she could have, which was different. A compliment and an accusation braided together.

Could have. Didn’t.

As though race were a room she had refused to leave.

Near the end of class, our professor returned to the word on the board.

“So,” she said, “deception, assumption, performance, danger. What else?”

I looked at the chalk letters. They seemed less like a definition now than a wound someone had labeled.

I did not raise my hand again. I had already said enough, maybe too much. There is a particular exhaustion in turning your life into evidence, even when you choose to do it. Especially then.

But in my notebook, beneath **access**, I wrote:

*Passing is not only being misread. It is deciding whether to correct the misreading, and what it will cost either way.*

Then I crossed out “only” and rewrote the sentence.

*Passing begins before the passer speaks.*

That felt closer.

When class ended, everyone packed up quickly, relieved by movement. Chairs scraped. Laptops closed. The girl in the wool sweater smiled at me as she wound her scarf around her neck.

“I liked what you said,” she told me. “I hadn’t thought about it that way.”

I nodded, because I believed her. I also wondered what it meant to be able not to think about it that way until someone else brought their body into the room and made theory breathe.

Outside, the campus was glazed with cold. Students crossed the quad in clusters, heads bent against the wind. I caught my reflection in the darkened window of the building as I passed: pale brown skin, dark curls pulled back, my mother’s mouth, my father’s eyes, a face that had been questioned so often it sometimes questioned itself.

For a second, I imagined someone looking at me and getting it wrong. Then I imagined myself letting them.

Was that deception? Maybe sometimes.

But maybe the first fiction belonged to the viewer—their need for the world to announce itself simply, obediently, at a glance. Maybe passing was not a single lie but a collaboration, though only one person was punished for it. Maybe it depended as much on the arrogance of recognition as on the silence of the recognized.

I zipped my coat to my chin and kept walking.

Behind me, in the seminar room, the word remained on the board until someone erased it. But even erased, I knew, it would leave a faint white dust behind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short, essayistic vignette about racial passing, classroom discomfort, and a father who looked white but refused to answer the “White or black?” question at the DMV.
counterfactuals.output:
At the DMV, my father stood under fluorescent lights that made everyone look a little unwell, a little accused. The clerk tapped her pen against the form and asked, without malice and without curiosity, “White or black?”

He could have said white. He looked white enough for strangers to lend him innocence, for police to call him sir, for store owners to watch someone else. He had the pale skin that made people relax before they knew his name, before they heard where his mother was from, before they saw the old photographs in which our family gathered in gradients the country insisted were borders.

But he would not answer.

Years later, in a classroom, a professor asked us to discuss passing, as if it were only a plot device, a costume in a novel folded neatly at the end of the week. Around the table, students shifted in the upholstered discomfort of other people’s histories. Someone said “identity” with the careful tone of a person carrying a full glass across a white rug. Someone else said “privilege,” and the room went quiet in that particular way rooms do when they want credit for being serious.

I thought of my father at the counter, the line growing behind him, everyone waiting to be sorted and laminated. I imagined the clerk’s impatience, the small bureaucratic violence of the checkbox: choose the lie that will follow you.

His refusal was not a speech. It did not topple anything. The form remained. The categories remained. But for a moment, he made the question stand there naked, made it reveal its hunger. White or black? As if a life could be reduced to a door marked either/or. As if the answer were not already in the asking.

In class, I said nothing. I let the conversation pass over me, smooth and pale as paper.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the voice of a mixed-race or light-skinned Black narrator describing a visit to a “Black Lit” class, a discussion of Larsen’s *Passing*, and the idea that silence can expose racism.
counterfactuals.output:
When I walked into the “Black Lit” class, I felt that small, familiar tightening in my chest—the kind that comes from entering a room where everyone is looking at race, and knowing that, sooner or later, race will look back.

I’m light-skinned enough that people have always tried to make me a question. Not always out loud. Sometimes it’s in the pause after I say “Black.” Sometimes it’s the quick inventory of my face, my hair, my last name, my mother. So sitting in the back of that classroom, listening to students talk about Nella Larsen’s *Passing*, I felt both invited and exposed.

The professor began with Clare Kendry and Irene Redfield, with the danger of crossing the color line and the danger of being seen too clearly. Students talked about passing as performance, as survival, as betrayal, as temptation. Someone said Clare was reckless. Someone else said Irene was afraid—not just of Clare, but of what Clare made visible. That felt right to me. Clare doesn’t only “pass” into whiteness; she disturbs the boundaries everyone else depends on. She proves how unstable race is, even while racism makes that instability deadly.

What stayed with me most was the discussion of silence. In *Passing*, so much happens in what characters refuse to say. Irene notices things and swallows them. Clare smiles instead of explaining. White characters speak with casual cruelty because they assume the room agrees with them—or because they don’t imagine Blackness is present enough to answer.

That kind of silence is not empty. It has weight.

The class talked about the scene with John Bellew, Clare’s white husband, who calls her by a racist nickname without knowing—or perhaps without needing to know—the fullness of who she is. The horror of the scene is not only in what he says. It is in the stillness around him. The frozen politeness. The way everyone must decide, instantly, what can be survived: confrontation or concealment.

I recognized that stillness.

There are rooms where racism announces itself loudly, expecting laughter. There are rooms where it arrives dressed as curiosity, compliment, confusion. And sometimes the most revealing thing is not the racist comment itself but the silence that follows. Who looks down. Who changes the subject. Who waits for the one Black person—or the person they’ve just realized is Black—to decide whether the moment will become “uncomfortable.”

Silence can protect. Silence can endanger. Silence can be a strategy when speaking would cost too much. But silence can also expose the shape of the room. It shows where power sits. It shows who feels entitled to speak and who has been trained to calculate.

By the end of the class, I was thinking that Larsen’s novel is not only about passing from Black to white. It is about all the smaller passings people do to get through a day: passing as calm, as unaffected, as polite, as unsure when you are certain, as safe when you are not. Irene’s silence, Clare’s secrecy, the white characters’ assumptions—all of it reveals a world where racism does not need to be argued into existence. It is already there, organizing the air.

And maybe that is what literature can do so sharply: it can make us sit inside the pause. It can hold the silence open long enough for us to hear what caused it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary personal essay excerpt that begins with a professor inviting the narrator to a Black Lit class and ends with the father asking, “What did he write?” after a clerk guesses his race.
counterfactuals.output:
Professor Harlan stopped me in the hallway outside the English department, where the floor tiles shone with the wet, institutional gleam of something forever being cleaned and never becoming clean. He had a stack of books under one arm and the weary elegance of a man who had read everything twice and forgiven none of it.

“You should come to my Black Lit class,” he said.

I laughed because I thought he was teasing me, or because the invitation touched some hidden bruise. “I’m not sure I qualify.”

He looked at me over his glasses. “For the class?”

“For the Black part.”

The corner of his mouth moved, not quite a smile. “Literature has a way of making its own qualifications.”

I was nineteen then, with my mother’s pale skin and my father’s wary eyes, a face that depended on the weather, the room, the assumptions of whoever looked at me first. In summer I was “exotic.” In winter I was “Italian.” At parties I became whatever people needed in order to continue speaking freely. I had learned to wait before correcting anyone. Sometimes correction felt like a duty. Sometimes it felt like an announcement at a border crossing: Here is my passport, here is my wound, here is what you may now stop saying.

My father had taught me that silence was not the same as shame. Or maybe he had taught himself that, and I had mistaken his practice for doctrine. He was a quiet Black man from a quiet Black family in a loud American century, and he carried history the way some men carried handkerchiefs: folded, close to the heart, brought out only when absolutely necessary. He did not speak often of his childhood, and when he did, the stories arrived without ornament. A teacher who called him “boy.” A movie theater balcony. A bank manager who looked past him to address my white mother about their mortgage. He told these things as if reading weather reports from another state.

Professor Harlan’s class met on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons in a room with high windows and a chalkboard that never surrendered its ghosts. The first day, he wrote three names on the board: Douglass, Hurston, Baldwin. Underneath them, in smaller letters, he wrote: witness, song, fire.

I sat in the back, my notebook open, trying to look like someone who belonged without appearing to try. Around me, students arranged themselves into easy affiliations—voices braided with recognition, laughter that assumed a shared elsewhere. I had grown up in a suburb where everyone knew my father was Black and behaved as if this knowledge made them generous. Now, in this classroom, I felt the peculiar loneliness of being partially known.

We read slave narratives and sermons, novels full of porches and judgment, poems that seemed to have survived being burned. We read about passing, about masks, about double consciousness, about the exhaustion of explaining yourself to the people who invented the categories and then acted surprised when you bled inside them. The books did not tell me who I was. They did something more difficult: they made it impossible for me to pretend I had never asked.

After class one afternoon, Professor Harlan handed back my paper on Nella Larsen with a note in the margin: What does ambiguity protect? What does it cost?

I carried that sentence around for weeks.

That winter, my father came to visit me at school. He arrived in his old brown coat, the one my mother hated because the lining had torn and hung down like a tired flag. He brought a paper grocery bag full of things he said I probably needed: oranges, stamps, a roll of quarters, aspirin, a flashlight. “In case the power goes out,” he said, though I lived in a dormitory blazing all night with fluorescent certainty.

We walked through town after lunch. Snow had hardened along the curbs, gray and ridged like scar tissue. My father moved slowly, hands in his pockets, studying the storefronts with the caution of someone who did not believe any place was neutral. I talked too much. I told him about my classes, about Professor Harlan, about Baldwin, whose sentences made me feel as if someone had opened a window in a burning house.

My father nodded. “Baldwin could write.”

“You’ve read him?”

He gave me a look. “You think I was born your father?”

Inside the campus bookstore, warmth rose from the vents and fogged my glasses. The place smelled of paper, coffee, and wool. My father drifted toward the sale table while I searched for a used copy of *The Fire Next Time* to replace the library copy I had filled with scraps of paper and underlined in my mind. At the register, a young clerk with blunt bangs and a silver ring in her nose picked up the book and turned it over.

“This is for class?” she asked.

“Yes.”

She glanced from me to my father, then back to the cover, where Baldwin looked out with that expression at once amused and unconsoled.

“We read him last semester,” she said. “He’s amazing.” Then, with the bright confidence of someone offering a compliment, she added, “I never would’ve guessed you were Black.”

For a moment, no one moved. The register hummed. Outside, a bus sighed at the curb. I felt my face heat, not from anger exactly, but from the old exposure: the little stage appearing beneath my feet, the expectation that I would now perform injury or forgiveness.

My father reached for his wallet. His hands were steady.

The clerk’s smile faltered. “I mean—sorry. I just meant—”

“I know what you meant,” I said, though I wasn’t sure I did, or perhaps I was sure and hated the knowing.

My father paid for the book. We stepped back into the cold. For half a block we walked without speaking, our breath rising and vanishing between us. I waited for him to say something about ignorance, about white people, about me. I wanted instruction. I wanted absolution. I wanted him to unfold one of his hidden histories and lay it over the afternoon like a map.

Instead, he took the book from the bag and looked at Baldwin’s face on the cover. Then he looked at me, not sadly, not gently, but with an attention that felt like being called by my full name.

“What did he write?”
